analysis.one_liner: Conditions federal airport grants on paying airport service workers at least $15 an hour with prevailing benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2023 with 16 cosponsors but never received a committee hearing or a vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require airports of any meaningful size to pay their service workers—security officers, cleaners, baggage handlers, food and retail staff, ticketing agents—at least $15 an hour, or the local prevailing wage if higher, plus required benefits. The way it enforces this is through money: an airport could not receive federal grants for runway, terminal, and other projects, including funding from the 2021 infrastructure law, unless it certifies every year that all service workers at the airport, including those hired through contractors, are paid accordingly. It never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Hundreds of thousands of airport service workers—baggage handlers, cabin cleaners, security officers, wheelchair assistants, food and retail staff, ticketing agents—would gain a guaranteed wage floor of at least $15 an hour or the local prevailing wage, plus fringe benefits, including workers employed through subcontractors. Travelers also benefit indirectly, since the bill's stated purpose is to reduce turnover and improve airport safety and service quality by stabilizing this workforce.

how_it_helps.text: It requires airport sponsors to ensure every covered service worker is paid at least the highest of $15/hour, the local Service Contract Act prevailing wage, federal contractor minimums, or state/local minimums, plus comparable fringe benefits.
The Labor Department must set occupation-by-occupation wage and benefit determinations for airport work within 90 days and update them annually, so the floor rises with local prevailing standards.
It reaches workers hired through contractors and subcontractors regardless of the contractual chain, closing the common loophole where staffing intermediaries employ the workers.
It leaves in place any state or local law requiring higher wages or benefits, so stronger local protections are not weakened.

analysis.who_pays: Airports and the airlines, contractors, and concession companies that employ service workers would bear higher wage and benefit costs, and would take on annual certification and reporting duties; they could pass some of this on through airport prices.

drawbacks.text: The wage-and-benefits floor applies only to small, medium, and large hub airports and only as a condition of federal project funding, so non-hub airports and potentially some funding pathways escape the requirement.

Higher wage and fringe-benefit mandates raise costs for airport operators, airlines, and concession companies; those costs could be passed on through higher airport retail and food prices or by cutting positions, and airports would carry new annual certification and compliance-reporting paperwork.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is real and direct: a firm wage-and-benefits floor for the mostly low-wage airport service workforce, tied to the federal grant money those airports already take. The cost falls on airport operators, airlines, and concessionaires, who would pay higher wages and benefits; some of that may pass through to airfares and airport prices, and airports would face new annual certification paperwork. On balance this is a straightforward redistribution from airport-related businesses and travelers to low-wage workers, and its main flaw is procedural: it was never considered.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from the day it was introduced until the two-year Congress ended, without a hearing, a markup, or any floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 9, 2023 and the Senate's only action was to read it twice and refer it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never held a hearing or vote, and the full Senate never considered it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Because bills do not carry over between Congresses, the bill expired and would have to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airport operators and the contractors that employ airport service workers are better off, since they avoid the higher wage and benefits costs and new compliance requirements. Workers who would have received a raise get nothing.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote the wage-certification mechanism tying federal airport funding to worker pay.

for.name: 16 Senate cosponsors (15 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and several committee members.

against.name: Airports and airline/airport-service industry groups
against.what_they_did: Industry groups generally oppose conditioning federal airport grants on wage mandates; no organized Senate opposition appears in the record because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced past referral in the Senate Commerce Committee.

industries.industry: Airport service workers (security officers, cleaners, baggage and ramp handlers, concession, food service, and ticketing staff)
industries.note: The bill would guarantee them a wage-and-benefits floor of at least $15/hour or the prevailing Service Contract Act standard, including workers employed through subcontractors. These are mostly low-wage workers, so the floor could materially raise their pay.

Airports would face higher labor costs from their contractors and new annual certification duties, and could lose federal grants if they do not certify compliance. The burden falls mostly on the operators of large public airports that receive federal money.

industries.industry: Airlines, ground-handling, and airport concessions and food service companies
industries.note: These firms employ most covered workers through contractors and would bear the increased wage and benefit costs; they could pass some through in prices charged at the airport.
